title: Comparison of arsenite and cadmium: Metal homeostasis and cellular stress response in human bronchial cells
projectDescription: Human exposure to cadmium and inorganic arsenic persists despite declining environmental levels. A proteomic profiling with label-free quantification was used to characterize the most abundant changes in protein expression after arsenite and cadmium exposure in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B) for 24 h. Both treatments induced protein expression related to cellular and oxidative stress pathways. In addition, cadmium exposure led to a stronger, more pronounced induction of metallothioneins. The dataset enables comparison of compound-specific proteomic responses to cadmium and arsenite and provides insight into differential regulation of oxidative stress and metal homeostasis pathways. In addition, the data highlights both similarities and discrepancies between transcriptional and protein-level responses after 24 h of exposure. This dataset serves as a resource for studying heavy metal-induced toxicity and supports integrative multi-omics analyses.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Cells (10⁶ per sample) were cultured in 6 cm dishes for 24 h and treated in biological triplicates with NaAsO₂ or CdCl₂ for 24 h. After treatment, cells were washed and harvested. Cell pellets were washed three times with 1 mL ice-cold PBS. For protein extraction, cell pellets were lysed in buffer containing 7 M urea, 2 M thiourea, 5 mM DTT, and 2% CHAPS for 15 min on ice. Samples were sonicated (30 s total, 10 s pulses, 10 % amplitude) and centrifuged (20,000 g, 15 min) to remove debris. Protein concentration was determined using a 660 nm assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For sample preparation, 10 kDa molecular weight cut-off filters (Nanosep, Pall) were used. Per sample, 20 µg protein were loaded onto pre-conditioned filters (1 % formic acid). Notably, after every incubation or washing step, the filters were centrifuged for 15 min at 12,000 g. Washing steps were performed with urea buffer (8 M Urea, 100 mM Tris, pH 8.5). Proteins were reduced with 8 mM DTT (15 min at 56 °C) and alkylated using 50 mM IAM (20 min, room temperature). Further, IAM was quenched using 8 mM DTT (15 min at 56 °C). Buffer exchange was performed using 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC). Proteins were digested on-filter using trypsin (0.01 µg/µL in ABC) overnight at 37 °C. Peptides were eluted by centrifugation. Samples were acidified to 0.2% TFA and dried completely. Peptides were reconstituted in 2 % acetonitrile (ACN) and 0.1 % formic acid (FA). Peptide concentration was determined at 205 nm. Approximately 200 ng peptides were injected into an UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano system coupled to a Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The solvents used were 0.1 % FA in water (A) and 0.1 % FA in ACN (B). First, a trapping column was used with a flow rate of 8 µL/min for 5 min and 100 % solvent A. As an analytical column, bioZenPeptide XB-C18, 2.6 μM, 250 μM x 0,075 mm column (Phenomenex) with a flow rate of 0.3 µL/min and a temperature of 40°C was used. A linear gradient was set as follows: 2 % B at 0 min, 34 % B at 60 min, 100 % B from 62 to 65 min, and 2 % B from 66 to 80 min. The analytical column was directly coupled to a Nanospray Flex ion source. The ion spray voltage was set to 1.7-2.0 kV, the capillary temperature to 250 °C, and the S-lens level to 60. The data were generated using a Top20 data-dependent acquisition (DDA) approach in a positive electrospray ionization mode. The isolation width was set to 2 m/z with a normalized collision energy of 28% and a charge of +2. For a full scan at the MS1 level, the resolution was set to 70,000, the automated gain control (AGC) to 3e6, the scan range to 360-1300 m/z, and the maximal injection time to 50 ms. For MS2 scans, only ions with the charge of +2 to +7 were analyzed. The resolution was set to 17,000, the AGC target to 1e5, and the maximum injection time to 50 ms. The MS2 spectra were recorded with a fixed first mass of 140 m/z and a dynamic exclusion time of 15 s. The total method runtime was 80 min.
dataProcessingProtocol: The MaxQuant software (version 2.4.2.0) was used to identify peptides and proteins from the human proteome. The human proteome was obtained from the UniProt Database (FASTA file download, October 25th, 2021; UP000005640). As fixed modifications, carbamidomethylation on cysteine (+57.02), and as variable modifications, oxidation of methionine (+15.99) and the N-terminal protein acetylation (+42.01) were set. Intensity-based absolute quantification (IBAQ) was used for label-free quantification. IBAQ values from each sample were summarized and normalized to a control sample using a normalization factor. Further, proteins identified only by site, reverse identifications, and typical contaminants were removed. The MaxQuant evaluations were done separately for each independent experiment. The software Perseus (version 2.0.10.0) was used for further data processing. The data were filtered for proteins with IBAQ values in at least two of the three biological replicates. Missing values were imputed from a normal distribution.
